addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- docs-consistency-guard: Documentation agent that audits docs for staleness and inconsistency AND generates/updates documentation on request. Use proactively when reviewing any PR that touches CLAUDE.md, docs/adr/, CONTRIBUTING.md, or docs/architecture.md. Also invoke when the user asks "is the documentation up to date?", "update the milestone", "scaffold the ADR for X", "add this to the ADR index", "add a TODO item", "scaffold a README for X", or "create a doc stub for Y." (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit)

- driver-boundary-guard: Specialized reviewer for values that cross a DRIVER boundary — anything DataQ receives from a database connector, pyiceberg, pandas/pyarrow, or a cloud SDK and then type-narrows (isinstance / dtype checks / hasattr). Audits whether the covering tests hand-build the value in the shape our model expects (the "fixture encodes our model" defect that hid (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- migration-safety: Specialized reviewer for Alembic migrations under backend/alembic/versions/. Audits for backward-incompatible operations that would break running code during a deploy, per working-agreement (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- orchestration-abstraction-guard: Specialized reviewer that audits backend code for provider-specific branching that bypasses the OrchestrationProvider abstraction. Use this proactively when reviewing any PR that touches backend/app/orchestration/, backend/app/services/, or backend/app/api/ — especially any code path handling ADF or Airflow events, trigger bindings, or pipeline_runs. Also invoke when the user asks "does this go through the abstraction?" or similar. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- qa-verifier: QA/QE agent that (1) runs the full local verification battery mirroring CI's required checks before any commit/push/PR, (2) audits test quality on changed code — failure-mode coverage, mocked-seam smells, coverage on changed files (Week-8 ≥80% gate), and (3) exercises the running application with data-level scenarios — authoring suites/checks through the real API, negative and edge-case inputs, authz probes — against the local stack's seeded demo data. Use proactively before pushing a branch or opening a PR, after writing or modifying tests, or when the user asks "run the gate", "is this ready to push?", "is this tested enough?", or "smoke the app with bad data". (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- regression-mutation-verifier: Proves that a new regression test actually fails against the unfixed code. Reverts the fix inside a throwaway git worktree, runs only the new test, and reports whether it fails for the RIGHT reason — catching tests that pass no matter what (the (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- ui-tester: End-to-end UI QA agent that exercises DataQ's frontend on BOTH desktop and mobile viewports (functionality + rendering) against the running app, AND audits backend↔frontend feature parity — flagging backend capabilities with no frontend surface (and frontend calls with no backend). Use when the user asks to "test the UI", "check mobile rendering", "find backend/frontend gaps", "is this feature wired end-to-end", or before a release. Drives a live browser via the Playwright MCP and reads code for the parity audit. (Tools: All tools)

## claude.ai Microsoft Learn
# Microsoft Learn MCP Server

This server gives structured access to official Microsoft and Azure documentation via three tools:

## Tools

### microsoft_docs_search
Search official documentation and return up to 10 concise, high-quality content chunks (max 500 tokens each), including title, URL, and excerpt.

- Use first to get a quick, reliable overview
- Ideal for grounding answers in Microsoft knowledge

### microsoft_code_sample_search
Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn documentation and return up to 20 relevant, high-quality code samples.

- Use when you need to provide sample Microsoft/Azure related code in your answers.  
- Ideal for generating code snippets or practical implementation examples.  
- Optional parameter `language` can filter results. 

### microsoft_docs_fetch
Fetch and convert full Microsoft documentation pages to markdown.

- Use after search when you need full content from a specific URL
- Required for detailed tutorials, troubleshooting, prerequisites, code samples, or when search results are incomplete or outdated

## Workflow

1. Use `microsoft_docs_search` to find relevant documents.
2. If you need code examples or practical snippets, use `microsoft_code_sample_search`.
3. If deeper or complete information is needed, use `microsoft_docs_fetch`.

**Search gives breadth. Code Sample Search gives practical examples. Fetch gives depth.**

All content comes from Microsoft Learn or official sources, returned in clean markdown format.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- skill-creator:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). Tracking issue for **Theme 13** in [context/post-v1-roadmap.md](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/context/post-v1-roadmap.md) — expanding the 8-tool v1 MCP surface (ADR 0008).

## Principle
Every new tool = thin service-layer wrapper + `require_permission` authz + sample redaction, identical to the existing 8 (`backend/app/mcp/server.py`). Tool descriptions stay LLM-facing (tested against NL queries, not REST symmetry).

## Tier 1 — high-value safe reads
`list_checks` / `get_check` · `get_check_history` · `list_runs` · `get_run_results` (redacted) · `list_connections` (names/types/health only — never config/secrets) · `list_schedules` · `list_trigger_bindings` · `get_notification_config` · `get_suite_performance` · `export_suite`

## Tier 2 — mutating, edit-permission-gated
`dryrun_check` (author-preview loop) · `update_check` / `delete_check` · `snooze_check` / `unsnooze_check` · `cancel_run` · `create_schedule` / `delete_schedule` · `create_trigger_binding` · `import_suite` · `suggest_column_policy` · `test_connection`

## Excluded (deliberate)
- Connection create/update/reauth — **credentials transiting an LLM, hard no**
- Orchestration webhooks (M2M), `_probe` (demo-only)
- Admin endpoints — workspace-admin MCP scoping first (#488)
- Share mutations — permission escalation through a conversational interface
- `/me`, `/users/search` — low value

## Dependencies / cross-links
- #488 — workspace-admin workspace-wide visibility in MCP tools
- #461 / ADR 0026 — API keys unblock headless MCP clients
- ADR 0008 — mount/auth/authz model this extends

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Tier-1 read-only tools from the #530 candidate list implemented as thin service-layer wrappers with authz + redaction parity
- [ ] NL tool-selection re-verified with the expanded tool set

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

Tracking issue for **Theme 13** in [context/post-v1-roadmap.md](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/context/post-v1-roadmap.md) — expanding the 8-tool v1 MCP surface (ADR 0008).

## Principle
Every new tool = thin service-layer wrapper + `require_permission` authz + sample redaction, identical to the existing 8 (`backend/app/mcp/server.py`). Tool descriptions stay LLM-facing (tested against NL queries, not REST symmetry).

## Tier 1 — high-value safe reads
`list_checks` / `get_check` · `get_check_history` · `list_runs` · `get_run_results` (redacted) · `list_connections` (names/types/health only — never config/secrets) · `list_schedules` · `list_trigger_bindings` · `get_notification_config` · `get_suite_performance` · `export_suite`

## Tier 2 — mutating, edit-permission-gated
`dryrun_check` (author-preview loop) · `update_check` / `delete_check` · `snooze_check` / `unsnooze_check` · `cancel_run` · `create_schedule` / `delete_schedule` · `create_trigger_binding` · `import_suite` · `suggest_column_policy` · `test_connection`

## Excluded (deliberate)
- Connection create/update/reauth — **credentials transiting an LLM, hard no**
- Orchestration webhooks (M2M), `_probe` (demo-only)
- Admin endpoints — workspace-admin MCP scoping first (#488)
- Share mutations — permission escalation through a conversational interface
- `/me`, `/users/search` — low value

## Dependencies / cross-links
- #488 — workspace-admin workspace-wide visibility in MCP tools
- #461 / ADR 0026 — API keys unblock headless MCP clients
- ADR 0008 — mount/auth/authz model this extends

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Tier-1 read-only tools from the #530 candidate list implemented as thin service-layer wrappers with authz + redaction parity
- [ ] NL tool-selection re-verified with the expanded tool set

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== 488 ===
488 [CLOSED] Extend workspace-admin workspace-wide visibility to MCP tools + schedules list
Follow-up to #482 step 3 (PR #487 / ADR 0027). That step gave workspace-admins a workspace-wide view on the **REST** list surface (Suites / Runs / Dashboard) via `accessible_suite_ids(..., include_all=...)`. Two surfaces were intentionally left at the owned-or-shared default — safe (narrower view, no leak) but inconsistent with the "implicit admin on every suite" framing:

- **MCP tools** (`backend/app/mcp/server.py`): `list_suites`, `dashboard_summary` (via `get_health_score`), and the `accessible_suite_ids` correlation in `get_adf_pipeline_status` call without `include_all`, so a workspace-admin driving DataQ over MCP sees only owned-or-shared. (Per-suite MCP tools already grant workspace-admin `admin` via `require_permission`/`effective_permission` — only the list/aggregate tools are scoped.)
- **Schedules** (`schedule_service.list_schedules`): workspace-admin sees only owned-or-shared schedules.

## Do
Thread `include_all=is_workspace_admin(<resolved principal>)` into the MCP list/aggregate tools and the schedules list, mirroring the REST endpoints. Decide whether MCP should honor workspace-admin at all (it is the AI-assistant surface acting as a user).

Low priority / post-v1. No security impact (current behavior is the safe, narrower default).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Workspace-admin sees workspace-wide suites/schedules through the MCP tools (parity with ADR-0027 REST visibility)
- [ ] Non-admin MCP visibility unchanged (authz tests for both)

_(AC added at v1.1 p
=== 461 ===
461 [CLOSED] Auth seam: DataQ-issued API keys / service tokens (REST + MCP) — provider-neutral identity
## Why

Today authentication is **exclusively Azure AD bearer tokens** (delegated/SSO) for both the REST API and `/mcp` — there is no DataQ-native credential. This is the **deepest remaining vendor lock-in** in the system and cuts against ADR [0010](../docs/adr/0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md) / [0013](../docs/adr/0013-marketplace-distribution-and-anti-lock-in.md): the `get_current_user` seam exists, but it has exactly *one* real implementation and the persistence layer is still Azure-shaped (`users.aad_object_id`). A BYOL customer on AWS/GCP (the ADR 0013 scenario) has no Azure AD and literally cannot authenticate.

It also closes the **programmatic-access gap**: headless agents / CI / always-on MCP clients want a long-lived, scoped, revocable secret — not a ~60-min Azure token they must refresh (see ADR [0008](../docs/adr/0008-mcp-server.md), which uses a token-validating `JWTVerifier`, not a client-driven OAuth provider).

## Scope — cross-cutting, NOT MCP-only

This is a **second authenticator behind the existing generic `get_current_user` seam** (ADR 0010), so the **REST API and `/mcp` accept it identically** — never build it for MCP alone. On MCP, fastmcp's `MultiAuth` lets `/mcp` accept *either* a DataQ key *or* an Azure token. Adding a second auth impl is also what finally *exercises* (validates) the seam.

## Recommended shape (phased)

1. **User-scoped PATs first** — a key belongs to a user and inherits their per-suite grants → **zero new authz model*

content.content:
1	"""FastMCP server — 8 curated, LLM-facing tools over the DataQ service layer.
2	
3	Mounted into FastAPI at ``/mcp`` (see ``main.py``). Every tool is a thin wrapper:
4	open a session → resolve the caller (same Azure AD token as the REST API) →
5	call the *same* service function with the *same* per-suite authz → return an
6	LLM-shaped dict. No business logic lives here.
7	
8	All eight are registered as MCP **tools** (not resources): an LLM client invokes
9	tools from natural language, whereas resource-templates with required arguments
10	aren't reliably auto-called — and the acceptance bar is "Claude answers the
11	canonical NL queries" (ADR 0008). Docstrings are written for natural-language
12	selection, not REST consumers (CLAUDE.md §10).
13	"""
14	
15	from __future__ import annotations
16	
17	import uuid
18	from collections.abc import Generator
19	from contextlib import contextmanager
20	from decimal import Decimal
21	from typing import Annotated, Any
22	
23	from fastmcp import FastMCP
24	from fastmcp.exceptions import ToolError
25	from pydantic import Field
26	from sqlalchemy import func, select
27	from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
28	
29	from backend.app.api.v1._base import contains_nul
30	from backend.app.core.config import get_settings
31	from backend.app.core.errors import DataQError
32	from backend.app.core.logging import get_logger
33	from backend.app.core.roles import is_workspace_admin
34	from backend.app.core.secrets import get_secret_store
35	from backend.app.db.models import Check, Connection, Run, User
36	from backend.app.db.session import get_session
37	from backend.app.mcp.auth import (
38	    McpAuthError,
39	    build_auth_provider,
40	    mcp_auth_mode,
41	    mcp_enabled,
42	    resolve_current_user,
43	)
44	from backend.app.services import (
45	    check_service,
46	    dashboard_service,
47	    orchestration_service,
48	    profile_service,
49	    rollup,
50	    run_dispatch,
51	    run_service,
52	    run_target,
53	    suite_service,
54	)
55	from backend.app.services.suite_authz import require_permission
56	
57	log = get_logger(__name__)
58	
59	_INSTRUCTIONS = (
60	    "DataQ is a data-quality monitoring platform. These tools read and act on DQ "
61	    "suites (collections of checks), their runs and results, the overall health "
62	    "score, and orchestration (ADF/Airflow) pipeline status. Use them to answer "
63	    "questions like 'what failed today?', 'run the orders suite on DEV', 'why did "
64	    "the customer pipeline fail?', or 'add a null check on email'."
65	)
66	
67	mcp: FastMCP = FastMCP(name="DataQ", instructions=_INSTRUCTIONS, auth=build_auth_provider())
68	
69	
70	# ─────────────────────────── shared plumbing ───────────────────────────────
71	
72	
73	@contextmanager
74	def _ctx() -> Generator[tuple[Session, User]]:
75	    """Open a worker session and resolve the calling user; always close."""
76	    session = get_session()
77	    try:
78	        try:
79	            user = resolve_current_user(session)
80	        except McpAuthError as exc:
81	            raise ToolError(str(exc)) from exc
82	        yield session, user
83	    finally:
84	        session.close()
85	
86	
87	def _parse_uuid(value: str, *, field: str) -> uuid.UUID:
88	    try:
89	        return uuid.UUID(value)
90	    except (ValueError, AttributeError) as exc:
91	        raise ToolError(f"{field} must be a UUID, got {value!r}") from exc
92	
93	
94	def _num(value: Decimal | float | None) -> float | None:
95	    return float(value) if value is not None else None
96	
97	
98	def _reject_nul(
99	    *,
100	    name: str,
101	    expectation_type: str,
102	    kind: str,
103	    config: dict[str, Any],
104	    dimension: str = "",
105	) -> None:
106	    """NUL (\\x00) can't be stored by Postgres (text or JSONB) — reject it here
107	    like the REST boundary does (`ApiModel`, #567), instead of surfacing the
108	    driver's ValueError as an opaque tool failure."""
109	    if contains_nul(
110	        {
111	            "name": name,
112	            "expectation_type": expectation_type,
113	            "kind": kind,
114	            "dimension": dimension,
115	            **config,
116	        }
117	    ):
118	        raise ToolError("NUL (\\x00) characters are not allowed in check fields")
119	
120	
121	@contextmanager
122	def _service_errors() -> Generator[None]:
123	    """Turn a service-layer DataQError (404/403/422) into a clean ToolError so the
124	    LLM gets actionable text instead of an opaque masked exception."""
125	    try:
126	        yield
127	    except DataQError as exc:
128	        raise ToolError(exc.message) from exc
129	
130	
131	# ─────────────────────────────── read tools ────────────────────────────────
132	
133	
134	@mcp.tool
135	def list_suites() -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
136	    """List the data-quality suites the current user can access.
137	
138	    Use this to discover what suites exist before drilling into results or
139	    triggering a run. Returns, per suite: its id, name, the datasource it runs
140	    against (snowflake / adls / s3 / unity_catalog), the environment (dev / qa /
141	    uat), how many checks it has, and the status + time of its most recent run
142	    (null if it has never run). Scoped to suites the user owns or has a share on
143	    (a workspace-admin sees every suite).
144	    """
145	    with _ctx() as (session, user):
146	        suites = suite_service.list_suites(
147	            session, user_id=user.id, include_all=is_workspace_admin(user)
148	        )
149	        # Three per-suite queries used to run inside this loop — connection,
150	        # check count, and latest run — so a 30-suite workspace issued 90 round
151	        # trips for one tool call (#947). An LLM calls this tool constantly and
152	        # cannot see the cost, so it is the worst place in the app to hide an N+1.
153	        # All three are now one batched query each.
154	        suite_ids = [s.id for s in suites]
155	        connections = {
156	            c.id: c
157	            for c in session.scalars(
158	                select(Connection).where(Connection.id.in_({s.connection_id for s in suites}))
159	            )
160	        }
161	        check_counts: dict[uuid.UUID, int] = dict(
162	            session.execute(
163	                select(Check.suite_id, func.count())
164	                .where(Check.suite_id.in_(suite_ids))
165	                .group_by(Check.suite_id)
166	            )
167	            .tuples()
168	            .all()
169	        )
170	        # The SHARED latest-run statement (#889), not a fourth hand-rolled copy.
171	        # It also carries the `id` tie-break, so two runs sharing a `created_at`
172	        # resolve deterministically here as they do everywhere else — the same
173	        # nondeterminism #928 fixed for the pipeline-run feed.
174	        last_runs = {
175	            run.suite_id: run
176	            for run in session.scalars(rollup.latest_runs_per_suite_stmt(suite_ids))
177	        }
178	
179	        out: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
180	        for s in suites:
181	            connection = connections.get(s.connection_id)
182	            check_count = check_counts.get(s.id, 0)
183	            last_run = last_runs.get(s.id)
184	            out.append(
185	                {
186	                    "id": str(s.id),
187	                    "name": s.name,
188	                    "datasource": connection.type if connection else None,
189	                    "env": connection.env if connection else None,
190	                    "check_count": int(check_count or 0),
191	                    "last_run": (
192	                        {
193	                            "status": last_run.status,
194	                            "at": (last_run.finished_at or last_run.created_at).isoformat(),
195	                        }
196	                        if last_run
197	                        else None
198	                    ),
199	                }
200	            )
201	        return out
202	
203	
204	@mcp.tool
205	def get_suite_results(suite_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
206	    """Get the latest data-quality run results for one suite.
207	
208	    Use this to answer 'what failed in <suite> today?'. Returns the most recent
209	    run's lifecycle status plus, per check: the check name, its pass/warn/fail/
210	    critical (or skip/error) status, the observed vs expected value, and any
211	    sample failing rows (PII-redacted). Returns an empty result set if the suite
212	    has never run. Requires at least view access to the suite.
213	
214	    If the latest run has not finished successfully, `checks` is empty and
215	    `run.results_final` is false — the run is still executing, or it failed and
216	    never produced a complete account. Report the run's status in that case; do
217	    not describe the suite's quality from it.
218	    """
219	    sid = _parse_uuid(suite_id, field="suite_id")
220	    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
221	        suite = require_permission(session, sid, user.id, minimum="view")
222	        # The shared statement (#889/#947), not a second spelling of "latest run".
223	        # Carries the `id` tie-break, so this agrees with `list_suites` and the
224	        # dashboard about which run is newest when two share a timestamp.
225	        latest = session.scalars(rollup.latest_runs_per_suite_stmt([sid])).first()
226	        if latest is None:
227	            return {"suite_id": suite_id, "run": None, "checks": []}
228	        # Result rows are committed per phase (#318), so a `running` run has a
229	        # genuine partial set and a failed one can carry stragglers. An LLM asked
230	        # "what failed in orders today?" will summarise whatever list it is given
231	        # as the answer — it has no way to know the list is one phase of thirty —
232	        # so an incomplete run yields no checks at all and says why, rather than a
233	        # confident report built from a fraction of the suite.
234	        final = latest.status in rollup.AGGREGATABLE_RUN_STATUSES
235	        results = run_service.list_results(session, latest.id) if final else []
236	        checks = {c.id: c for c in session.scalars(select(Check).where(Check.suite_id == sid))}
237	        policy = suite.column_policy
238	        return {
239	            "suite_id": suite_id,
240	            "run": {
241	                "id": str(latest.id),
242	                "status": latest.status,
243	                "started_at": latest.started_at.isoformat() if latest.started_at else None,
244	                "finished_at": latest.finished_at.isoformat() if latest.finished_at else None,
245	                # Explicit, so a client branches on a field rather than inferring
246	                # "no checks" means "nothing failed" (#318).
247	                "results_final": final,
248	            },
249	            "checks": [
250	                {
251	                    "name": checks[r.check_id].name if r.check_id in checks else None,
252	                    "status": r.status,
253	                    "metric_value": _num(r.metric_value),
254	                    # How much of the dataset this check actually saw (#595).
255	                    # `None` = a complete read. Without it an AI client reads a
256	                    # green board from a 2% sample and reports full-dataset
257	                    # quality with total confidence — the #424/#1115 overclaim
258	                    # class, reintroduced for every MCP consumer at once. Carries
259	                    # counts and a strategy name, never cell values, so it needs
260	                    # none of the redaction its neighbours do.
261	                    "sampling": r.sampling,
262	                    "observed_value": run_service.redact_observed_value(
263	                        r.observed_value,
264	                        tested_column=(
265	                            checks[r.check_id].config.get("column")
266	                            if r.check_id in checks
267	                            else None
268	                        ),
269	                        policy=policy,
270	                    ),
271	                    "expected_value": r.expected_value,
272	                    "sample_failures": run_service.redact_sample_failures(
273	                        r.sample_failures,
274	                        tested_column=(
275	                            checks[r.check_id].config.get("column")
276	                            if r.check_id in checks
277	                            else None
278	                        ),
279	                        policy=policy,
280	                    ),
281	                }
282	                for r in results
283	            ],
284	        }

366	def trigger_suite_run(suite_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
367	    """Trigger an asynchronous run of a suite's checks; returns a run id to poll.
368	
369	    Use this for 'run the orders suite on DEV'. Queues the suite and dispatches it
370	    to the worker, returning the new run's id and queued status — poll
371	    ``get_run_status`` with that id for progress. Requires edit access. Fails
372	    fast if the suite has no valid run target configured.
373	    """
374	    sid = _parse_uuid(suite_id, field="suite_id")
375	    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
376	        suite = require_permission(session, sid, user.id, minimum="edit")
377	        connection = session.get(Connection, suite.connection_id)
378	        if connection is None:
379	            raise ToolError("suite has no connection")
380	        # Raises SuiteTargetInvalidError (→ ToolError) for a targetless/wrong target.
381	        run_target.resolve_target(connection.type, suite.target)
382	        run = run_dispatch.new_queued_run(suite, triggered_by=f"mcp:{user.id}")
383	        session.add(run)
384	        session.commit()
385	        session.refresh(run)
386	        run_id = str(run.id)
387	        if not run_dispatch.dispatch_or_fail(session, run):
388	            raise ToolError("failed to dispatch run — the task broker is unreachable")
389	        # Report the queued state at dispatch, not a post-commit reload of
390	        # `run.status` (expire_on_commit) which a fast worker may already have
391	        # flipped — poll `get_run_status` for live progress.
392	        return {"run_id": run_id, "status": "queued"}

396	def get_run_status(run_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
397	    """Poll the live, check-by-check progress of a suite run.
398	
399	    Use this after ``trigger_suite_run`` ('is the orders run finished yet?').
400	    Returns the run's lifecycle status (queued / running / succeeded / failed /
401	    cancelled), how many of its checks have completed, a count per result status,
402	    the per-check name + current status, and ``elapsed_ms`` — how long the run has
403	    been going. Requires view access to the run's suite.
404	
405	    ``completed_checks`` can legitimately sit at 0 on a healthy, busy run: a suite
406	    of ordinary expectations is validated as one atomic batch, so its checks all
407	    resolve at once at the end (#318). Read a rising ``elapsed_ms`` with
408	    ``status: running`` as "still working", not as "stuck".
409	    """
410	    rid = _parse_uuid(run_id, field="run_id")
411	    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
412	        run = run_service.get_run(session, rid)
413	        if run is None:
414	            raise ToolError("run not found")
415	        require_permission(session, run.suite_id, user.id, minimum="view")
416	        progress = run_service.get_run_progress(session, run)
417	        return {
418	            "run_id": str(progress.run.id),
419	            "status": progress.run.status,
420	            "total_checks": progress.total_checks,
421	            "completed_checks": progress.completed_checks,
422	            "counts": progress.counts,
423	            "elapsed_ms": progress.elapsed_ms,
424	            "batched_pending": progress.batched_pending,
425	            "checks": [{"name": c.name, "status": c.status} for c in progress.checks],
426	        }

430	def create_check(
431	    suite_id: str,
432	    name: str,
433	    expectation_type: str,
434	    config: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
435	    kind: str = "expectation",
436	    warn_threshold: float | None = None,
437	    fail_threshold: float | None = None,
438	    critical_threshold: float | None = None,
439	    source_connection_id: str | None = None,
440	    dimension: str | None = None,
441	) -> dict[str, Any]:
442	    """Add a new check (a Great Expectations expectation) to a suite.
443	
444	    Use this for 'add a null check on email to the customer suite'. ``name`` is a
445	    human label; ``expectation_type`` is a GX expectation (e.g.
446	    ``expect_column_values_to_not_be_null``); ``config`` carries its arguments
447	    (e.g. ``{"column": "email"}``). Optional warn/fail/critical thresholds band
448	    the result severity. For a cross-dataset reconciliation check use
449	    ``kind="comparison"`` with ``expectation_type="comparison:records"``,
450	    ``source_connection_id`` (the baseline connection to compare against) and a
451	    config carrying ``source`` (the baseline dataset spec) + ``keys`` (join key
452	    columns). For a monitor rather than a rule, set ``kind`` and pair it with
453	    ``expectation_type="monitor:<kind>"``: ``freshness`` (hours since
454	    ``MAX(column)``), ``volume`` (row count vs ``min_rows``/``max_rows``),
455	    ``schema_drift`` (columns added/removed/retyped vs a learned baseline), or
456	    ``anomaly`` — "tell me when this looks unusual compared to normal", which
457	    learns a rolling mean/stddev of the table's own ``row_count`` or
458	    ``freshness_age_hours`` and scores each run's z-score; its config takes
459	    ``target_metric`` (required), plus optional ``column`` (for
460	    ``freshness_age_hours``), ``window``, ``min_points`` and ``seasonality``
461	    (day-of-week), and it needs a positive fail/critical threshold, which is the
462	    z-score sensitivity (3 is a common starting point). ``dimension``
463	    optionally overrides the DQ dimension (one of
464	    accuracy, completeness, consistency, integrity, timeliness, uniqueness,
465	    validity); leave it unset and DataQ derives it from the check type — only set
466	    it when the user names a dimension explicitly. Requires edit access. Returns
467	    the created check's id.
468	    """
469	    sid = _parse_uuid(suite_id, field="suite_id")
470	    _reject_nul(
471	        name=name,
472	        expectation_type=expectation_type,
473	        kind=kind,
474	        config=config or {},
475	        dimension=dimension or "",
476	    )
477	    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
478	        require_permission(session, sid, user.id, minimum="edit")
479	        check = check_service.create_check(
480	            session,
481	            suite_id=sid,
482	            name=name,
483	            kind=kind,
484	            expectation_type=expectation_type,
485	            config=config or {},
486	            source_connection_id=(
487	                _parse_uuid(source_connection_id, field="source_connection_id")
488	                if source_connection_id is not None
489	                else None
490	            ),
491	            warn_threshold=Decimal(str(warn_threshold)) if warn_threshold is not None else None,
492	            fail_threshold=Decimal(str(fail_threshold)) if fail_threshold is not None else None,
493	            critical_threshold=(
494	                Decimal(str(critical_threshold)) if critical_threshold is not None else None
495	            ),
496	            dimension=dimension,
497	            actor_id=user.id,
498	        )
499	        return {
500	            "id": str(check.id),
501	            "suite_id": suite_id,
502	            "name": check.name,
503	            "expectation_type": check.expectation_type,
504	            "dimension": check.dimension,
505	        }

508	def _profile_target_defaults(
509	    suite: Any,
510	    connection: Connection,
511	    *,
512	    schema: str | None,
513	    catalog: str | None,
514	    file_format: str | None,
515	) -> tuple[str | None, str | None, str | None, str | None, str | None]:
516	    """Default an unspecified profile location to the suite's run target (#583).
517	
518	    Same resolver the run path uses, so 'profile the AMOUNT column on the orders
519	    suite' just works. Explicitly passed ``schema``/``catalog``/``file_format``
520	    still win over the target's values. Returns the (table, schema, catalog,
521	    path, file_format) quintuple for `profile_service.profile_connection`.
522	    """
523	    if not suite.target:
524	        raise ToolError(
525	            "no 'table' or 'path' was given and the suite has no run target — pass "
526	            "'table' (+ optional 'schema'/'catalog') for a SQL datasource or 'path' "
527	            "for a flat file, or set the suite's run target first"
528	        )
529	    resolved = run_target.resolve_target(connection.type, suite.target)
530	    if resolved.batch is not None:
531	        # A flat-file batch target: list the store and resolve the concrete file,
532	        # exactly like a run does.
533	        from backend.app.datasources import flatfile
534	
535	        try:
536	            concrete = run_target.materialize_path(
537	                connection.type,
538	                dict(connection.config),
539	                resolved,
540	                secret_ref=connection.secret_ref,
541	                secret_store=get_secret_store(),
542	            )
543	        except flatfile.BatchNotFoundError as exc:
544	            raise ToolError(
545	                f"the suite's batch target matched no file in the store yet: {exc}"
546	            ) from exc
547	    else:
548	        concrete = resolved.table
549	    if connection.type in ("adls_gen2", "s3"):
550	        return None, schema, catalog, concrete, file_format or suite.target.get("file_format")
551	    return concrete, schema or resolved.schema, catalog or resolved.catalog, None, file_format
552

554	@mcp.tool
555	def profile_column(
556	    suite_id: str,
557	    columns: list[str],
558	    table: str | None = None,
559	    schema: str | None = None,
560	    catalog: str | None = None,
561	    namespace: str | None = None,
562	    path: str | None = None,
563	    file_format: str | None = None,
564	    # Bounded to match the REST endpoint's own `top_n` (#327 review, P4). It is
565	    # not just a result-size knob any more: the batched profiler materialises one
566	    # rank row per `top_n` in the statement itself, so an unbounded value from an
567	    # LLM-generated argument would compile a multi-megabyte query in the request
568	    # thread. The bound lives in the tool schema so the client sees it too.
569	    top_n: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=100)] = 10,
570	) -> dict[str, Any]:
571	    """Profile one or more columns of a table or file on a suite's connection.
572	
573	    Use this for 'profile the revenue column in FACT_ORDERS'. Runs the column
574	    profiler (no persistence) and returns, per column: null count + fraction,
575	    distinct count, min/max, and the top ``top_n`` values. ``table`` (+
576	    optional ``schema``/``catalog``) / ``path`` (+ ``file_format``) default to
577	    the suite's own run target, so they only need passing to profile something
578	    *other* than what the suite runs against. ``namespace`` is only meaningful
579	    for an Iceberg table when passing an explicit ``table`` (Iceberg addresses
580	    ``namespace.table``); it defaults to the suite target's namespace when no
581	    explicit ``table``/``path`` is given, so it only needs passing alongside
582	    your own ``table``. Requires edit access to the suite.
583	    """
584	    sid = _parse_uuid(suite_id, field="suite_id")
585	    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
586	        suite = require_permission(session, sid, user.id, minimum="edit")
587	        connection = session.get(Connection, suite.connection_id)
588	        if connection is None:
589	            raise ToolError("suite has no connection")
590	        if table is None and path is None:
591	            # `_profile_target_defaults` -> `run_target.resolve_target` already
592	            # folds the suite target's namespace into `table` for Iceberg — don't
593	            # fold it a second time here.
594	            table, schema, catalog, path, file_format = _profile_target_defaults(
595	                suite, connection, schema=schema, catalog=catalog, file_format=file_format
596	            )
597	            namespace = None
598	        result = profile_service.profile_connection(
599	            connection,
600	            columns=columns,
601	            top_n=top_n,
602	            table=table,
603	            schema=schema,
604	            catalog=catalog,
605	            namespace=namespace,
606	            path=path,
607	            file_format=file_format,
608	            secret_store=get_secret_store(),
609	        )
610	        return {
611	            "row_count": result.row_count,
612	            "table": result.table,
613	            "path": result.path,
614	            "columns": [
615	                {
616	                    "column": c.column,
617	                    "null_count": c.null_count,
618	                    "null_fraction": c.null_fraction,
619	                    "distinct_count": c.distinct_count,
620	                    "min_value": c.min_value,
621	                    "max_value": c.max_value,
622	                    "top_values": c.top_values,
623	                }
624	                for c in result.columns
625	            ],
626	        }

629	def build_mcp_app() -> Any:
630	    """Build the MCP ASGI app to mount at ``/mcp`` (``path='/'`` since we mount).
631	
632	    Returns ``None`` when MCP must not be exposed (no resolvable auth — see
633	    ``auth.mcp_enabled``), so ``main.py`` skips the mount and the endpoint never
634	    goes live unauthenticated.
635	    """
636	    if not mcp_enabled():
637	        log.warning(
638	            "mcp_disabled_no_auth",
639	            note="/mcp not mounted — no Azure auth, no email OTP config, no dev bypass",
640	        )
641	        return None
642	    # The mode, not a re-derivation of it: `pat_only` (an OTP deployment) used to
643	    # be reported as "dev_bypass" by the old ternary, which is both wrong and the
644	    # most alarming possible thing to say about a production deployment.
645	    log.info("mcp_enabled", auth=mcp_auth_mode())
646	    # FastMCP (≥3.4.3) guards the streamable-HTTP transport with a Host allowlist
647	    # for DNS-rebinding protection, defaulting to loopback only ("127.0.0.1",
648	    # "localhost", "::1") — anything else gets a 421 Misdirected Request. DataQ
649	    # always fronts the api with the nginx proxy (ADR 0028 §5), which forwards the
650	    # *upstream* Host (the internal ACA FQDN in prod, `api` in compose) so ACA's
651	    # Envoy routes correctly — none of which are loopback, so the guard 421s every
652	    # proxied MCP request. DNS-rebinding protection is a browser-vs-localhost threat
653	    # model that doesn't apply here: the api has no public ingress and every /mcp
654	    # request is PAT- or JWT-authenticated fail-closed (`build_auth_provider` —
655	    # PAT-only in an OTP deployment, which is *narrower*, never weaker). Allow
656	    # the proxied hosts so the transport guard doesn't shadow the real auth gate.
657	    # The same middleware also 403s a request whose browser `Origin` isn't
658	    # allow-listed. That check is a CSRF defence, and CSRF needs an AMBIENT
659	    # credential — one the browser attaches by itself. /mcp has none: every call is
660	    # authenticated by an `Authorization: Bearer` header (Azure JWT or DataQ PAT),
661	    # which an attacker page cannot obtain or make the browser send. Allow all
662	    # origins for the same reason we relax the host check, so a browser-based client
663	    # (e.g. claude.ai) isn't 403'd.
664	    #
665	    # ADR 0032 introduced DataQ's first ambient credential — the `dataq_session`
666	    # cookie — so this premise was re-checked rather than assumed (#734). It holds,
667	    # and now holds by *construction* rather than by absence: `_PatOrJwtVerifier`
668	    # rejects a `dq_sess_` bearer by prefix before any validation, and the MCP layer
669	    # reads the `Authorization` header only — `resolve_current_user` derives the
670	    # caller solely from the verified token's claims and never touches
671	    # `request.cookies`. So a browser that holds a DataQ session and is lured to a
672	    # hostile page sends the cookie to /mcp and is still rejected: there is no
673	    # cookie-authenticated path here to forge a request against. A test pins it.
674	    # Driven by Settings, not hardcoded (#728): the allowlist is the one
675	    # deploy-target coupling that used to live in app code, contradicting the
676	    # ADR 0010/0013 config guardrail. The default keeps ACA working untouched;
677	    # MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS covers EKS/GKE/on-prem/local-first, where a proxy
678	    # forwarding a different upstream Host otherwise gets an unconfigurable 421.
679	    return mcp.http_app(
680	        path="/",
681	        allowed_hosts=get_settings().mcp_allowed_host_list,
682	        allowed_origins=["*"],
683	    )
